quick.topic: Test the code, not the world
quick.summary: Why your pipeline tests break for the wrong reasons, and how to fix it.
quick.takeaway: Pass external tools into your code so you can easily swap them for tests.

parts.title: Test the code, not the world

beats.line: My test failed because the remote storage was down. Is my code bad?

board.text: Test the code, not the world

beats.line: Not necessarily. You are testing a car in heavy city traffic.
So the test broke because of the traffic, not the engine?
Right. We want to test the engine on a closed track.
To do that, we swap the real storage for a fake version.
In testing, we call this a mock object.
Can I just say a fake thing we control?
You can. A fake thing always replies exactly how you want.
That sounds great, but how do I actually swap it out?

parts.cliff: How to swap the fake in.

beats.line: Think of your code like a lamp with a standard plug.
So I do not wire it directly into the wall?
Exactly. You pass the power source in from the outside.
By passing the storage tool in, you can change it easily.
So in production, I pass the real remote storage plug?
Yes. And in your test, you plug in your fake version.
Your engine does not know the difference. It just runs.
I write the code to take any plug, then pass a fake one.
Now your tests only fail when your engine actually breaks.

quiz.question: What is the main benefit of using a fake thing in your tests?
options: It isolates your code so tests do not fail from outside issues.
It creates automatic documentation for your pipelines.
It makes your real production systems run twice as fast.
It stores the data permanently on your local computer.
quiz.explanation: A fake thing replaces unpredictable outside systems so you only test your own logic.

quiz.question: To use a fake thing easily, you should hardcode external connections inside your logic.
quiz.explanation: You should pass connections in from the outside. That way, you can plug in a fake one during testing.
